newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Clinton win would bring relief in Moscow - experts.
newsitem.headline: Clinton win would bring relief in Moscow - experts.

text.p: Moscow will breathe a sigh of relief if President Bill Clinton is re-elected on Tuesday but Russian-U.S. relations face testing times whatever the outcome, Russian foreign policy experts said on Monday.
The Kremlin has not expressed any official preference for Clinton or Republican rival Bob Dole in the U.S. presidential election.

But President Boris Yeltsin's good personal ties with "my friend Bill", Moscow's desire for continuity and its mistrust of the Republicans ensure that the Kremlin will be leaning towards Clinton behind the scenes.

"If everything goes the way it seems to be going, Clinton will be re-elected and there will be a sigh of relief in Moscow -- in the foreign ministry and in the Kremlin," independent political analyst Andrei Kortunov told Reuters.
"Moscow feels Clinton has invested a lot in Russia and that this would make it more difficult for him than for Dole to make a sudden change in U.S. policy."

Continuity will be particularly important for the Kremlin in the next few months when, if all goes well, Yeltsin will still be recovering from heart surgery or, in a worst-case scenario, Russia will be looking for his successor.
Russian eyes are focussed firmly on domestic problems and not on foreign policy.
"Some of Dole's comments are regarded here as having as an anti-Russian subtext and the Kremlin would not be happy if he won," said Pavel Kandel of Moscow's independent Institute of Europe thinktank.
"What Russia wants now, as before, is to maintain friendly relations with the United States."
Yeltsin and Clinton have had a warm personal relationship since reaching a "psychological understanding" at their first full summit in the Canadian city of Vancouver in April 1993.

Clinton has been a firm backer of Russian reforms and has stood behind Yeltsin when the going got tough, including resisting pressure to take a tougher stance against Moscow's military campaign to crush separatists in rebel Chechnya.

But although the two presidents have continued to give each other bear hugs in public, the euphoria of the period immediately after the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 has given way to a more perfunctory relationship dogged by problems.
On many issues, Moscow and Washington have simply chosen to agree to differ for the sake of keeping relations on track.
"The period of romanticism of Russia becoming a democratic state and part of the Western alliance is over," said Viktor Kremenyuk, deputy director of the independent USA and Canada Institute.
"Clinton looks likely to win and I don't think the election will change anything dramatically. But I foresee a devolution of the relationship towards cooler ties."

A major problem in the 1990s has been NATO's plans, backed by the United States, to take in countries of eastern and central Europe. Russia says this expansion would threaten its security and strongly opposes it.

This looks set to remain the major problem if Clinton wins a second four-year term and it could come to a showdown soon. Clinton said last month he was committed to trying to bring some former communist states into NATO by 1999.
"A Clinton victory would mean no major change in policy but this would also mean that the same problems we have now will continue. Above all this means NATO expansion," Kandel said.
NATO expansion could put in doubt Russian commitment to some arms treaties and prompt Moscow to push harder for closer ties with China and other former Soviet republics.
It would be likely to increase the trend towards a more nationalistic foreign policy in Russia.
But most independent analysts see little chance of a return to the Cold War days.

U.S. officials say Clinton will do nothing to jeopardise ties with Yeltsin. They also say they are confident that if Yeltsin is no longer president they have sufficient contacts with other Russian officials to keep the relationship on track.

Even if Dole came to power, the Kremlin would be sure to work equally hard to keep relations smooth. His election might even hold a silver lining for Moscow if the Republicans proved less committed to NATO enlargement than Clinton.
"A Dole victory need not lead to crisis and a quick worsening of relations," said Kremenyuk. "The Republicans are pragmatic people interested in pragmatic solutions."
